text: One chart answers one question. A real analysis needs several charts side by side, so a reader can compare them and see the whole picture. In Python, a dashboard is, at its core, a well-planned grid of charts.

plt dot subplots with rows and columns returns a figure and an array of axes. With one row, axes is one-dimensional, so index with axes zero, axes one. With several rows and columns, it's two-dimensional: axes row, column. sharey equals True makes panels use the same scale, which is what keeps side-by-side comparisons honest.

Here, average spend by segment and by region, side by side with a shared y-axis. Same spend scale on both, so the reader compares heights fairly instead of being misled by two different ranges, echoing the truncated-axis warning from lesson four.

Dashboards rarely use equal-sized panels. fig dot add_gridspec lets one axes span several cells. gs zero, colon means row zero, every column, so the revenue trend spans the whole top row, with three smaller charts beneath it.

The result reads as one view: a trend on top, then segment spend, the spend distribution, and orders versus spend below. Consistent color, left-aligned titles, and layout equals constrained, which keeps titles and labels from overlapping, make four separate charts feel like one dashboard.
Plotly's make_subplots does the same thing, and the panels stay interactive. Choose the grid with rows and cols, then add each trace with a row and col position, using go dot Bar and go dot Scatter.

Five dashboard principles: one question per panel, the most important chart top-left, consistent scales and colors throughout, shared axes for real comparisons, and stop at roughly six panels. That completes chapter two. Next: chapter three, the EDA mindset and workflow.
